To get rid of the spiciness when making something with raw onion i mix the cut up onion with salt in a bowl and let it rest for 10 minutes or so (the longer the better, cutting the onion into smaller pieces speeds this up) this draws out moisture and slightly softens them up as well. When i'm dicing an onion and i get to the bottom half i start cutting diagonally towards the center, this makes it so that the onion doesn't move as much when i'm cutting it (the pieces that are held together by the root part tend to get squeezed apart close to the end, especially if you are dicing it finely). When an onion starts to go bad the juice from the foul part spreads quickly through the space between the layers so it's better to remove the whole layer instead of just cutting out the foul part since the whole layer might be affected even if you can't see it from the outside. To not cry as much when dicing onions i prepare them all by making the vertical cuts on the onions first and then cutting them horizontally when i need them, this also saves space compared to just dicing them all beforehand.

Finally!  Addressing dicing onions non-generically.  Here's my twist:  
I also angle my polar cuts, and do not make a horizontal cut.  Instead, 
adjusting to the size of the onion,  I make 3-4 spaced-out cuts TO the 
board (rather than to ~.6 below).  Then,  I make shallower cuts in 
between these,  only half way down to the board.  For a particularly 
large onion,  I will even make cuts in between these,  going down only  
a few layers.   This avoids making those tiny pieces in the center.  
I also angle my orbital cuts. At the stem end, this keeps  the onion 
from becoming splayed.  At the stem end,  it keeps me from needing 
to flip the stub over,  as you showed.   All of this gives me that equal  
dice necessary for even cooking,  with the fewest moves.  Speaking 
of that,  I noticed that you used a board scraper to move the bulk of 
the product into a bowl,  and then to sweep the remaining amount in.  
Why not just slide your cutting board forward a little,  and rake it all in 
with your knife?   This uses (and washes) only one implement,  and 
keeps your fingers and your hand towel cleaner. -- Feel free to share.
